platforms.title: That Mouse or Keyboard Might Be Causing Tennis Elbow
platforms.meta_description: Elbow pain but you don't even play tennis? How the AAOS tells tennis elbow apart from golfer's elbow, by where it hurts and which motion triggers it.
platforms.body_html:
Elbow pain even though you've never played tennis in your life? The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) explains that tennis elbow and golfer's elbow involve tendons on exactly opposite sides of the elbow. The sport names are just labels — in practice, repetitive wrist motion from everyday habits is a far more common cause than either sport.

Why the names are sports but the causes are everyday habits

Tennis elbow is tiny, accumulated damage in the tendon of the muscle that bends the wrist backward, attached on the outer side of the elbow. A tennis backhand is the classic trigger, but using a computer mouse for long stretches, certain keyboard postures, and repetitive wrist extension like painting cause the exact same problem.

Golfer's elbow comes from the tendon on the completely opposite side. It's marked by tiny, accumulated damage in the tendon of the muscles that flex the wrist and grip the fingers, attached on the inner side of the elbow. A golf swing, gripping objects forcefully, and throwing motions commonly cause it.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether the pain sits on the outer or inner side of the elbow. The AAOS notes this is the single most reliable way to distinguish them. Outer-side pain leans toward tennis elbow, while inner-side pain leans toward golfer's elbow.

Second, which wrist motion makes it worse. Pain that flares when bending the wrist backward or lifting something points toward tennis elbow, while pain that flares when flexing the wrist or gripping tightly points toward golfer's elbow.

What matters most is not just resting and icing it without changing anything else. Without cutting back on the repetitive motion that's causing the damage, the pain tends to come right back no matter how much rest is taken. Steroid injections ease pain temporarily but can weaken the tendon with repeated use, so they aren't recommended as a first-line treatment — eccentric strengthening exercises that slowly stretch and build up the tendon offer a far more fundamental path to recovery.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether the pain is on the outer or inner side, which wrist motion makes it worse, and what repetitive activity has been happening recently. If it doesn't improve after a few weeks of managing it, or gets worse instead, seeing physical therapy or an orthopedic specialist is the safe move.

Equipment and setup matter more than most people expect. A mouse or keyboard positioned too far away, a tennis racket grip that's the wrong size, or tools with handles that force the wrist into an awkward angle all keep loading the same tendon over and over, undoing whatever progress rest and exercise manage to make. Adjusting the setup itself is often just as important as any exercise routine.

It's also worth mentioning any numbness or tingling that spreads into the fingers, since that combination points toward a pinched nerve near the elbow rather than a straightforward tendon problem, and it changes what kind of exam and treatment actually helps.

Is the pain you're feeling on the outer side of your elbow, or the inner side?
